opening.text: A sculptor looks at a rough block of stone and sees what it can become. She does not rush. She takes off a little at a time. Dust falls. Slowly, a shape appears. The stone does not do the work. But it has to stay on the table and let the sculptor shape it.
God sees what we can become, too. He is patient with us. I would like to talk about becoming like Jesus Christ.

mainMessage.text: The Lord wants each of us to become like His Son. That is not a small goal, and it does not happen all at once. It begins in the heart. It grows step by step. It shows in how we love and serve. We will stumble along the way. But God is patient, and the Savior helps us. Over time, we are changed.

blocks.text: We are meant to become like Him.

The apostle John wrote that when the Savior appears, we will be like Him. The Savior Himself told the Nephites to be perfect, even as He and the Father are perfect. It is a high goal. It is also a loving one. It is the very reason we are here.
Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is.
Therefore I would that ye should be perfect even as I, or your Father who is in heaven is perfect.
Elder Bruce R. McConkie of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in the priesthood session of the April 1982 general conference. The Ensign page is May 1982, page 34.

\[The doctrine of the priesthood\] is that we have power, by faith, to govern and control all things, both temporal and spiritual; to work miracles and perfect lives; to stand in the presence of God and be like him because we have gained his faith, his perfections, and his power, or in other words the fulness of his priesthood.
The promise is that we can stand in His presence and be like Him.
He knows what we can become.

The sculptor sees the finished work before she begins. The Lord sees us that way too. He said His work and His glory is to bring to pass our immortality and eternal life. And Paul taught that we are children of God, and heirs with Christ.
For behold, this is my work and my glory—to bring to pass the immortality and eternal life of man.

The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God: And if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together.
Elder Neal A. Maxwell of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles wrote this in his book Even As I Am, page 18. It is a book, not a conference talk.

Unlike our love, Jesus’ love consists of active restraint as well as pressing encouragement. His perfect love of each and all spares Him the need to accept us as we now are, for He knows perfectly what we have the possibility to become.
He loves us as we are. And He sees what we can be.
It begins in the heart.

Changing our behavior is part of it. But the Lord asks for more. He wants to give us a new heart. King Benjamin taught that the natural man gives way as we yield to the Holy Spirit and become, as a child, humble and full of love. Ezekiel said the Lord would give us a new heart and take away the stony one.

For the natural man is an enemy to God, and has been from the fall of Adam, and will be, forever and ever, unless he yields to the enticings of the Holy Spirit, and putteth off the natural man and becometh a saint through the atonement of Christ the Lord, and becometh as a child, submissive, meek, humble, patient, full of love, willing to submit to all things which the Lord seeth fit to inflict upon him, even as a child doth submit to his father.
A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.
Elder David A. Bednar of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Clean Hands and a Pure Heart” from the October 2007 general conference.

The gospel of Jesus Christ encompasses much more than avoiding, overcoming, and being cleansed from sin and the bad influences in our lives; it also essentially entails doing good, being good, and becoming better. . . . This mighty change is not simply the result of working harder or developing greater individual discipline. Rather, it is the consequence of a fundamental change in our desires, our motives, and our natures made possible through the Atonement of Christ the Lord. Our spiritual purpose is to overcome both sin and the desire to sin, both the taint and the tyranny of sin.
We cannot do it by willpower alone. The Atonement changes our desires.
It happens a little at a time.

A statue does not appear in a day. The Lord promised that He will give to the faithful line upon line, precept upon precept. And even the Savior grew. Luke tells us that Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man. If He grew, we can expect to grow too.
For he will give unto the faithful line upon line, precept upon precept; and I will try you and prove you herewith.
And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man.
President Ezra Taft Benson wrote this in his article “A Mighty Change of Heart” in the October 1989 Ensign. It is a magazine article, not a conference talk.

Becoming Christlike is a lifetime pursuit and very often involves growth and change that is slow, almost imperceptible. . . . True repentance involves a change of heart and not just a change of behavior. . . . Most repentance does not involve sensational or dramatic changes, but rather is a step-by-step, steady, and consistent movement toward godliness.
Step by step. That is how most of us change.
We put on His kind of love.

Paul told the Colossians to put on mercy, kindness, humility, and patience, and to forgive as Christ forgave. Above all, he said, put on charity. Mormon taught that charity is the pure love of Christ. He urged us to pray with all the energy of our hearts to be filled with it, so that we may be like Him.

Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering; Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye. And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.

But charity is the pure love of Christ, and it endureth forever; and whoso is found possessed of it at the last day, it shall be well with him. Wherefore, my beloved brethren, pray unto the Father with all the energy of heart, that ye may be filled with this love, which he hath bestowed upon all who are true followers of his Son, Jesus Christ; that ye may become the sons of God; that when he shall appear we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is; that we may have this hope; that we may be purified even as he is pure. Amen.
Elder Jeffrey R. Holland of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Tomorrow the Lord Will Do Wonders among You” from the April 2016 general conference.

The Lord blesses those who want to improve, who accept the need for commandments and try to keep them, who cherish Christlike virtues and strive to the best of their ability to acquire them. If you stumble in that pursuit, so does everyone; the Savior is there to help you keep going. . . . Soon enough you will have the success you seek.
Charity is a gift we can ask for. And the Lord gives it to those who pray.
When we fall, we get back up.

Every sculptor makes a wrong cut at times. Every learner stumbles. The scriptures tell us that the just man falls seven times and rises up again. The prophet Micah said, “When I fall, I shall arise.” Falling is part of the road. Staying down is not.
For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief.
Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the Lord shall be a light unto me.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the First Presidency said this in his talk “The Point of Safe Return” from the April 2007 general conference.

The Atonement of Jesus Christ is the gift of God to His children to correct and overcome the consequences of sin. God loves all of His children, and He will never cease to love and to hope for us. . . . There is always a point of safe return; there is always hope.
He will never stop hoping for us. So we can keep going.

story.title: Peter and John before the leaders

blocks.text: Peter and John were fishermen. They had no formal training in the law or in speaking to rulers. Yet when they stood before the leaders in Jerusalem, something about them was clear.
Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.

The leaders did not say, “They went to a good school.” They said, “They had been with Jesus.” Time with the Savior changes a person. It shows in how we speak and act. That is how we become like Him. We spend time with Him in prayer, in the scriptures, and in following His example.

application.text: First, spend a few minutes with the Savior each day this week. Read a short passage about His life and ask, “What is one thing I can do like Him today?” Second, pick one Christlike quality, such as patience or kindness. Write it down, and watch for a chance to practice it. Third, when you stumble, do not give up. Say a short prayer, and try again.

Becoming like Jesus Christ works in a similar way. The more time we spend in His company, the more His ways become ours. I would like to talk about that.

story.title: A people who became one in Christ

blocks.text: After the Savior visited the Nephites, the people changed. They were not born that way. They had chosen to follow Him, and the change lasted.

And it came to pass that there was no contention in the land, because of the love of God which did dwell in the hearts of the people. And there were no envyings, nor strifes, nor tumults, nor whoredoms, nor lyings, nor murders, nor any manner of lasciviousness; and surely there could not be a happier people among all the people who had been created by the hand of God. There were no robbers, nor murderers, neither were there Lamanites, nor any manner of -ites; but they were in one, the children of Christ, and heirs to the kingdom of God.

The scripture says the love of God dwelt in their hearts. That love changed how they treated each other. They were happy. They were one. They had become, in a real sense, children of Christ. When many people choose His way, a whole community can change.

application.text: First, “live in the country” of Christ this week. Read about Him, pray to Him, and ask what He would do. Second, practice one Christlike word. Say a kind thing to someone each day. Third, when you make a mistake, laugh a little, forgive yourself, and begin again.

Becoming like Jesus Christ is much the same. Day by day, it is hard to see. Over a year, over ten years, the marks climb. I would like to talk about this growth.

mainMessage.text: God wants His children to become like His Son. It is the reason for the plan. It starts with a change of heart, and it grows by small steps. We learn to love as He loves. We get things wrong and get back up. And all the way along, the Savior and the Holy Spirit help us. We do not have to be there today. We only have to keep growing.

The door is open. We are invited to walk through it.
He sees the grown-up version of us.

A parent looks at a small child and sees both the child and the adult the child may become. God sees us that way. He said His work and glory is to bring to pass our immortality and eternal life. And Paul said we are God’s children and joint-heirs with Christ.

story.title: The people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi bury their weapons

blocks.text: These were Lamanites who had once been fierce and violent. After they came to know the truth, they made a covenant with God. They decided never to take up weapons again.

And now it came to pass that when the king had made an end of these sayings, and all the people were assembled together, they took their swords, and all the weapons which were used for the shedding of man’s blood, and they did bury them up deep in the earth. And this they did, it being in their view a testimony to God, and also to men, that they never would use weapons again for the shedding of man’s blood; and this they did, vouching and covenanting with God, that rather than shed the blood of their brethren they would give up their own lives; and rather than take away from a brother they would give unto him; and rather than spend their days in idleness they would labor abundantly with their hands. And thus we see that, when these Lamanites were brought to believe and to know the truth, they were firm, and would suffer even unto death rather than commit sin; and thus we see that they buried their weapons of peace, or they buried the weapons of war, for peace.

They did not just change their minds. They changed their lives. They buried what once defined them. And they chose to labor and give, instead of take. That is what becoming like Christ looks like. A new heart leads to new actions.

application.text: First, make your own “doorframe.” Write down one Christlike quality you want to grow in. Check on it once a week. Second, bury one “weapon,” such as a harsh word, a grudge, or a bad habit. Choose to put it away. Third, say a prayer for the pure love of Christ, as Mormon taught.

The path ends in His presence.
He knows we can walk it.

No one lays out a path unless they believe someone will walk it. The Lord believes in us. His work and glory is to bring to pass our immortality and eternal life. And Paul taught that we are children of God and heirs with Christ.
For behold, this is my work and my glory—to bring to pass the immortality and eternal life of man.

The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God: And if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together.
Elder Neal A. Maxwell of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles wrote this in his book Even As I Am, page 18. It is a book, not a conference talk.

Unlike our love, Jesus’ love consists of active restraint as well as pressing encouragement. His perfect love of each and all spares Him the need to accept us as we now are, for He knows perfectly what we have the possibility to become.
He knows what we can become. That is why He does not give up.
The first step is in the heart.

A path starts with a decision to go. In the gospel, the first step is a change of heart. King Benjamin taught that we put off the natural man when we yield to the Holy Spirit. Ezekiel said the Lord would give a new heart and remove the stony one.

For the natural man is an enemy to God, and has been from the fall of Adam, and will be, forever and ever, unless he yields to the enticings of the Holy Spirit, and putteth off the natural man and becometh a saint through the atonement of Christ the Lord, and becometh as a child, submissive, meek, humble, patient, full of love, willing to submit to all things which the Lord seeth fit to inflict upon him, even as a child doth submit to his father.
A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.
Elder David A. Bednar of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles taught this in his talk “Clean Hands and a Pure Heart” from the October 2007 general conference.

The gospel of Jesus Christ encompasses much more than avoiding, overcoming, and being cleansed from sin and the bad influences in our lives; it also essentially entails doing good, being good, and becoming better. . . . This mighty change is not simply the result of working harder or developing greater individual discipline. Rather, it is the consequence of a fundamental change in our desires, our motives, and our natures made possible through the Atonement of Christ the Lord. Our spiritual purpose is to overcome both sin and the desire to sin, both the taint and the tyranny of sin.
The Atonement does what willpower cannot.
The path is worn by repeating.

Every time we walk the same way, the trail gets clearer. The Lord gives to the faithful line upon line, precept upon precept. Even Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man.
For he will give unto the faithful line upon line, precept upon precept; and I will try you and prove you herewith.
And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man.
President Ezra Taft Benson taught this in his article “A Mighty Change of Heart” in the October 1989 Ensign. It is a magazine article, not a conference talk.

Becoming Christlike is a lifetime pursuit and very often involves growth and change that is slow, almost imperceptible. . . . True repentance involves a change of heart and not just a change of behavior. . . . Most repentance does not involve sensational or dramatic changes, but rather is a step-by-step, steady, and consistent movement toward godliness.
Small daily steps wear the path.
The path is paved with love.

As we walk, we learn to walk the way He walks. That means mercy, kindness, patience, and forgiveness. Paul said above all to put on charity. Mormon taught that charity is the pure love of Christ, and that we can pray to be filled with it.

Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering; Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye. And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.

But charity is the pure love of Christ, and it endureth forever; and whoso is found possessed of it at the last day, it shall be well with him. Wherefore, my beloved brethren, pray unto the Father with all the energy of heart, that ye may be filled with this love, which he hath bestowed upon all who are true followers of his Son, Jesus Christ; that ye may become the sons of God; that when he shall appear we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is; that we may have this hope; that we may be purified even as he is pure. Amen.
Elder Jeffrey R. Holland of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles taught this in his talk “Tomorrow the Lord Will Do Wonders among You” from the April 2016 general conference.

The Lord blesses those who want to improve, who accept the need for commandments and try to keep them, who cherish Christlike virtues and strive to the best of their ability to acquire them. If you stumble in that pursuit, so does everyone; the Savior is there to help you keep going. . . . Soon enough you will have the success you seek.
Love is the surface we walk on.
When we step off the path, we step back on.

Everyone wanders sometimes. The just man falls seven times and rises up again. Micah said that when we fall we will arise, and that the Lord will be a light to us in darkness. The path is still there.
For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief.
Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the Lord shall be a light unto me.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the First Presidency taught this in his talk “The Point of Safe Return” from the April 2007 general conference.

The Atonement of Jesus Christ is the gift of God to His children to correct and overcome the consequences of sin. God loves all of His children, and He will never cease to love and to hope for us. . . . There is always a point of safe return; there is always hope.
The way back is always open.

story.title: Saul meets the Lord on the road to Damascus

blocks.text: Saul was traveling to Damascus. He had been working against the followers of Jesus. On the road, something stopped him.

And as he journeyed, he came near Damascus: and suddenly there shined round about him a light from heaven: And he fell to the earth, and heard a voice saying unto him, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? And he said, Who art thou, Lord? And the Lord said, I am Jesus whom thou persecutest: it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks. And he trembling and astonished said, Lord, what wilt thou have me to do? And the Lord said unto him, Arise, and go into the city, and it shall be told thee what thou must do.

Saul’s question changed everything. “Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?” He was ready to be taught. President Benson said that stories like this are real but are the exception more than the rule. Most of us change slowly. But the question Saul asked is one we can ask each day. What wilt thou have me to do?

application.text: First, each morning this week, ask Saul’s question in prayer: “Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?” Then do the first thing that comes to mind. Second, notice a path you are already wearing, whether good or bad. Choose one to keep, and one to change. Third, when you step off, step back on. Do not wait for Monday.

We tend it with small, daily choices. We learn to love as He loves. When storms knock us down, He helps us stand again. Growth takes time. But it is real, and it is promised.

Therefore I would that ye should be perfect even as I, or your Father who is in heaven is perfect.

\[The doctrine of the priesthood\] is that we have power, by faith, to govern and control all things, both temporal and spiritual; to work miracles and perfect lives; to stand in the presence of God and be like him because we have gained his faith, his perfections, and his power, or in other words the fulness of his priesthood.
The promise is large. The seed is small. Both are true.
The gardener knows what the seed will be.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time about becoming more like Jesus Christ. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: The good Samaritan

blocks.text: A man was beaten and left half dead by the road. Two men passed by. Then a Samaritan stopped.

But a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on him, And went to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him. And on the morrow when he departed, he took out two pence, and gave them to the host, and said unto him, Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee. Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves? And he said, He that shewed mercy on him. Then said Jesus unto him, Go, and do thou likewise.

The Samaritan did what the Savior does. He saw a need, he felt compassion, and he acted. He stayed with the man and made sure he was cared for. Jesus ended with a simple charge: “Go, and do thou likewise.” That is how Christlike love grows. One act of mercy at a time.

application.text: First, pick one Christlike quality to tend this week, such as patience, kindness, or forgiveness. Write it where you will see it. Second, do one small act of mercy for someone, as the Samaritan did. Do it quietly. Third, pray each day for the pure love of Christ, and thank Him for the growth you cannot yet see.
